attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: 💡 Make sure the [set sprite image to] blocks are in the [on game update every ms] loop. Nothing will change in the simulator yet.
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:❓ Did you drag both [set sprite image to] blocks from the [on start] container block into the [on game update every ms] loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:💡 The ninja should not change the name of the sprite in the [set sprite image to] blocks, as they will do that in the next step.
steps.instructions:
Help the wizard collect the magical mushrooms! 


Open the Game code block menu then drag out an [on game update every ms] loop.


Drag both of the mushroom sprites’ [set sprite image to] blocks out of the [on start] container block into the [on game update every ms] loop.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add the green mushroom sprite image to the [set projectile to projectile from side] block and set vy to 0?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:❓ What do you notice about the velocity of the projectiles? How fast and in what direction are they moving?❓ What do you think might happen with the two different colored mushroom projectiles?


Sensei Pro Tip:💡Velocity refers to the speed of something moving in a certain direction. The projectiles should be moving from the left side of the screen to the right.
steps.instructions:
Make the mushrooms move across the screen.


Open the Sprites code block menu then drag a [set projectile to projectile from side] block into the [on game update every ms] loop, above the [set sprite image to] blocks.. 


Drag the green mushroom sprite image into the projectile image, then delete its [set sprite image to] block. Change the velocity values so the sprite moves across the screen from left to right, only.


Change the sprite name in the pink mushroom sprite’s [set sprite image to] block to projectile.


Click ▶ to see pink mushrooms move along the top of the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the sprite name in the [set sprite x to] block and change the coordinate axis from the drop down menu?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:❓ How does the [set sprite x to] block affect the sprite’s position? How is it similar and different from using the [set sprite position to] block?❓ Does your [pick random] block include values that include the entire height of the screen (0-120)?


Sensei Pro Tip:💡The ninja can use the [set sprite x to] when they want to set only the x or y value, such as setting the x position when a sprite is only moving up and down with direction buttons, or setting the y position for projectiles to always fall from the top of the screen.
steps.instructions:
Set the mushroom sprites’ y position so it starts at different vertical points before moving right across the screen.


Open the Sprites code block menu then drag a [set sprite x to] block into the [on game update every ms] loop below the [set projectile to projectile from side] block. Select the sprite name “projectile” in the red bubble, then select “y” from the drop down menu.


Open the Math code block menu then drag a [pick random] value block into the empty value bubble. Select the range of random y values, between 0 to 120, for the projectile sprite’s starting y position.


Click ▶ to see pink mushroom projectiles start at different y coordinate values and move across the screen.

steps.hints: 💡 While nothing will change in the simulator, be sure to check that you set the projectile’s sprite kind to Enemy after the [set projectile to projectile from side]. Then, set projectile sprite kind to Food after the pink mushroom [set sprite image to] block.
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:❓ How might the Player sprite interact differently with the Enemy and Food sprites? What do you think will happen?


Sensei Pro Tip:💡Explain to the ninja that they are setting up their code to include “good” (objects to collect) projectiles and “bad” (objects to avoid) projectiles by editing the sprite kinds.
steps.instructions:
Set the green mushroom projectile as the Enemy and the pink mushroom projectile as Food.


Open the Sprites code block menu then drag a [set sprite kind to] block into the [on game update every ms] loop below the [set projectile to projectile from side] block. Select the sprite name “projectile” in the red bubble, then set “Enemy” as the sprite kind.


Drag another [set sprite kind to] block into the [on game update every ms] loop below the [set sprite image to] block. Select “Food” as the sprite kind.

steps.hints:
❓ Did you replace <true> with the [%  chance] value block, then update the % parameter to 25?


﻿
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:❓ Which color mushroom appears more often on the screen? Why do you think so?❓ What would happen if you changed the [% chance] value to 10? 50?❓ Since the pink mushrooms are Food sprites, how might you make them appear more often on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:💡 Conditional refers to code that causes a program to make a decision. It requires an if statement to be true, in order for the code to run.💡A ninja may need help understanding percentages and probability. Guide the ninja to think about the number of times out of 100 (or 10, for simpler examples), that the projectile will be pink. In this example, the projectile will be pink 25 times out of 100.
steps.instructions:
Use a “coin toss” conditional to determine if a mushroom projectile is an Enemy or Food sprite!


Open the Logic code block menu then drag an [if true then] container block into the bottom of the [on game update every ms] loop. 


The [if true then] container block is a conditional. This means that the actions within the container block will run after a program makes a decision.  


Drag both of the pink mushroom projectile’s blocks into the [if true then] conditional.


Open the Math code block menu then drag a [% chance] value block into the <true> part of the [if true then] conditional. Type the number 25 into the bubble.


Click ▶ to see both green and pink mushroom projectiles move across the screen. Notice which color mushroom you see more often!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the wizard’s x value, then set the vx to 0 so it only moves up and down?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might you want the Player sprite to only be able to move up and down on the screen? What would you do if you wanted them to only move left and right?

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja to notice that the order of the code blocks matters. Any block that refers to a sprite needs to come after its [set sprite to] block.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to only move up and down on the right side of the screen.


Open the Sprites code block menu then drag a [set sprite x to] block into the [on start] container block. Select the Player sprite’s name in the block, then select an x value so the Player sprite is positioned on the right side of the screen.


Then, drag in a [move sprite with buttons] block and change the velocity values so the Player sprite can only move up and down. Set the Player sprite to stay in screen, too.


Click ▶ then use the up and down direction buttons to move the Player sprite on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the sprite kinds in the two [on sprite overlaps sprite] container blocks and use the otherSprite bubble in the [destroy sprite] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen differently when the Player overlaps with an Enemy sprite versus a Food sprite?

❓ Did you test out different effects and sounds and select ones that you like?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja to drag the otherSprite bubble into the [destroy sprite] block, so that the event happens when the Player overlaps with any sprite of a certain kind.

💡Remind the ninja to use Player as the first sprite kind in each [on sprie overlaps sprite] container block, then update the second kind to Enemy and Food.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when the Player sprite overlaps the Enemy and Food sprites!


Drag out two [on sprite overlaps sprite] container blocks. Use one event to set what happens when the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite, and another when the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite.


When the Player sprite overlaps either the Enemy or Food sprites, play a sound until done, then destroy the other Sprite.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Player sprite overlaps the Enemy and Food sprites.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you check where you set variables versus where you change variables?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:❓ What other variables could you add to this game to make it more exciting?


Sensei Pro Tip:💡 Guide the ninja to observe the placement of the [set score to] and [change score by] blocks to make sure they correspond with the correct events.
steps.instructions:
Add a score variable to your game!


Open the Info code block menu then drag out a [set score to] block into the [on start] container block. 


Next, drag out a [change score by] block into both [on sprite overlaps sprite] container blocks, after the destroy code, so the score increases when the Player overlaps Food, and decreases when the Player overlaps an Enemy.


Click ▶ to see the score change when the Player overlaps Food and Enemy sprites! Notice that the score only changes by 1 point on each interaction, after the Enemy and Food sprites have been destroyed.

steps.hints: ❓ Does your [if true then] conditional check if the score is equal to a certain value?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What might be a good score for a Player to reach to win the game, that makes it challenging but not too easy?

❓What do you notice about the [if true then] block? Why do you think it is helpful to use in a game?

❓ How does the Player win the game? When do they lose?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to tinker with the score value and the dropdown menu in the [0=0] value block to think about what other possibilities there are to end the game at a certain score.
steps.instructions:
End the game when the player reaches a certain score.


Open the Logic code block menu then drag an [if true then] conditional into the bottom of the Food sprite’s [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. Then, drag a [game over] block inside the [if true then] conditional.


Open the Logic code block menu then drag a [0=0] block into the <true> part of the [if true then] conditional. Open the Info code block menu then drag a (score) value block into the left side of the [0=0] value block. Then, type the number 10, or another high score, in the right side of the [0=0] value block.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Player collects 10 Food sprites!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add customizations to your game including a background color, screen effect, directions and more?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Which block will set a background color? Which block will set dialog boxes?

❓ What directions will help people understand how your project works?


﻿

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize your game with a background color or image and dialog boxes to provide game instructions.


Click ▶ to play your completed game!

subgroups.introduction: Create a game where the Player has to collect Food projectiles while avoiding Enemy projectiles. Win the game by collecting enough Food projectiles!

validationItems.text: Use a Game Update loop to create a Projectile from the side of the screen.
Code Projectile sprites to enter from a random y coordinate.
Set 1 Projectile sprite kind to Enemy, and set the other Projectile sprite kind to Food.
Use an if conditional statement with a percent chance value block to determine if a projectile is a Food sprite kind.
Set the Player sprite’s x coordinate, then code the Player sprite to only move up and down using the buttons.
Destroy the Food sprite and increase the score when it overlaps with a Player sprite.
Destroy the Enemy sprite and decrease the score when it overlaps with a Player sprite.
Add an if conditional statement that runs the Game Over (Win) function if the score variable is equal to a specific number.
Add a background color or image, sound effects, or dialog boxes with game directions.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Yellow Belt! In this level, you’ll learn about conditionals, which are code that makes a decision in a program. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: What if?
badges.description: Use conditionals to make different things happen in a project.

badges.title: To Be or Not to Be?
What are the Chances?
badges.description: Use probability in a conditional statement.

badges.title: Same Difference
badges.description: Compare two values in a conditional statement.

badges.title: Coming from Left Field
badges.description: Launch a projectile from the side of the screen.

badges.title: Weighing the Options
badges.description: Use an if/else statement in a project.
